cards.text: Welcome to Sparkle's station, friend! A new section of Proverbs opens here, and the heading reads, "The proverbs of Solomon:" That's Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, and his sayings come two lines at a time, putting the wise and the foolish side by side.

cards.question: Solomon starts with family. A wise son brings joy to his father. What does a foolish son bring his mother?

cards.text: Then Solomon talks money: "Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing." That's worth less than the dead batteries I shared my old junk drawer with, and at least THEY swore they had a little charge left!

cards.question: Crooked treasure profits nothing. What does Solomon say righteousness brings?
True or false: Solomon says the LORD lets the righteous go hungry.

cards.text: The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but He denies the craving of the wicked. Next, Solomon holds up two pairs of hands: idle ones and diligent ones.

cards.question: Idle hands make one ___, but diligent hands bring wealth.
Harvest time, two sons. One gathers in summer, and one sleeps through it. Which one does Solomon call a disgraceful son?

answers.text: The one who sleeps during harvest
The one who gathers in summer
The one who sells the harvest

cards.text: The sleeper! Harvest is the ONE season you do not hit snooze, and I say that as a stamper who snoozed an oven timer once and smelled it for a week. Then Solomon says blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.

cards.question: Solomon says the memory of the righteous is a blessing. What does he say happens to the name of the wicked?

cards.text: A wise heart will receive commandments, but foolish lips will come to ruin. And he who walks in integrity walks securely.

cards.question: Integrity walks securely. What does Solomon say happens to the one who perverts his ways?

cards.text: He who winks the eye causes grief, and then that line again: foolish lips will come to ruin. With eyebrows THIS big, I couldn't wink if I tried, so I'm in the clear on that one.
Next, the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, and hatred stirs up dissension. That's one comment in the group chat, and suddenly forty people are typing.

cards.question: Hatred stirs up dissension. What does Solomon say love does?

cards.text: Wisdom is found on the lips of the discerning, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks judgment. And the wise store up knowledge, like stocking up on chocolate chips before the holiday rush.

cards.question: The wise store up knowledge. What does Solomon say the mouth of the fool invites?

cards.text: Then Solomon gets real about money: the wealth of the rich man is his fortified city, but poverty is the ruin of the poor.

cards.question: Solomon compares what people get for their work. The labor of the righteous leads to ___, but the gain of the wicked brings ___.

cards.text: Back at the counter, friend. Solomon says whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life.

cards.question: Heeding instruction puts you on the path to life. What does Solomon say about the one who ignores reproof?

cards.text: Then Solomon says the one who conceals hatred has lying lips.

cards.question: Solomon says the one who hides hatred has lying lips. And whoever spreads slander is a ___.
Now Solomon turns to how much a person talks. What does he say happens when words are many?

cards.text: But he who restrains his lips is wise, and somebody needs to tape that RIGHT over the reply-all button. Then the tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth.

cards.question: Solomon says fools die for lack of judgment. What does he say the lips of the righteous do for many?
True or false: Solomon says the blessing of the LORD enriches, but sorrow comes along with it.

cards.text: The fool delights in shameful conduct, but a man of understanding has wisdom. Then Solomon says what the wicked man dreads will overtake him.

cards.question: What the wicked man dreads will overtake him. What does Solomon say about the desire of the righteous?
Then a whirlwind passes, and the wicked are no more. What does Solomon say about the righteous?

answers.text: They are scattered for a while
They rebuild from the ground up

cards.text: Then Solomon paints a picture that makes you squint: like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes.

cards.question: Vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes. Who does Solomon say is like that to those who send him?

cards.text: The slacker: the coworker who says "On it!" and then you never hear from him again. Next, the fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be cut short.

cards.question: Solomon says the expectations of the wicked will perish. What does he say the hope of the righteous is?

cards.text: The way of the LORD is a refuge to the upright, but destruction awaits those who do evil. And the righteous will never be shaken, but the wicked will not inhabit the land.

cards.question: Solomon says a perverse tongue will be cut out. What does he say the mouth of the righteous brings forth?

cards.text: The lips of the righteous know what is fitting, but the mouth of the wicked is perverse. Mouths, lips and tongues ALL over this chapter, friend, and here I am with a giant mustache parked right over mine like a filter!

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 3 quotes "Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Almost every choice card follows the same frame: Papa Dorin gives one half of a proverb, then asks for the other half ("X. What does Solomon say about Y?"). None of the cards ask what a proverb means, what its picture is, or what the chapter keeps coming back to (speech, work, the righteous and the wicked). Prep becomes a recall drill of line halves instead of a reading of the passage's meaning.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 7 of 10 choice cards are multiple choice, with 1 true or false and 2 fill in the blank. Most use the same "first half, then what does Solomon say about the second half" frame.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop even more: 8 of 10 choice cards are multiple choice, with 1 true or false and 1 fill in the blank. The stop repeats Stop 1's pattern of half-proverb setup, then a question about the other half.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The card is a bare recitation of verses 3 and 4 with no voice, and no reaction or comparison. The same goes for Stop 1 cards 11, 18 and the first sentence of 16, and Stop 2 cards 3, 9 and 16. In the stretches built from these cards, Papa Dorin reads like a verse list, not a funny storyteller.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Card 5 has just asked about Proverbs 10:3. This card then opens by restating it word for word ("The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry"), so it recaps the answered line instead of only moving forward.
The question sets up exactly two sons, one who gathers and one who sleeps. That rules out the third answer, "The one who sells the harvest," before the baker even thinks about it.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Blank 1 asks the baker to choose "life" over "rest," "honor" or "freedom." All four are positive results of righteous labor, so nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason to "life." It tests the verse's exact wording, which the baker hasn't seen.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Several story cards state proverbs in the exact BSB wording but without quotation marks, and often without saying Solomon is the speaker. In this card, "A wise heart will receive commandments, but foolish lips will come to ruin. And he who walks in integrity walks securely." reads as Papa Dorin's own statement. The same happens in Stop 1 cards 6, 13, 16 and 18, and Stop 2 cards 9, 16 and 18.
findings.question: When a story card uses the exact BSB wording, must it go in quotation marks and be attributed to the speaker, or may Papa Dorin say it unquoted as his own narration?
